column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 42: “Son of Ādam, so long as you call upon Me and hope in Me”

column2: From Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Allah the Exalted said: Son of Ādam, so long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I will forgive you whatever you have done, and I do not mind.

Son of Ādam, were your sins to reach the clouds of the sky and you then asked My forgiveness, I would forgive you. Son of Ādam, were you to come to Me with nearly an earthful of sins and then meet Me without associating anything with Me, I would come to you with nearly an earthful of forgiveness.”
Al-Tirmidhī reported it and said: A good (ḥasan) hadith.

Al-Tirmidhī alone recorded this hadith. He recorded it by way of Kathīr ibn Fāʾid: Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd told us: I heard Bakr ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Muzanī say: Anas told us — and he mentioned it. He said: Good and unusual (ḥasan gharīb); we know it only by this route. End of quotation.
Its chain is acceptable. Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd is al-Hunāʾī; Abū Ḥātim said of him: A shaykh.

Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him in al-Thiqāt, and whoever claims he is someone other than al-Hunāʾī is mistaken. Al-Dāraquṭnī said: Kathīr ibn Fāʾid alone narrated it from Saʿīd as marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ); Salm ibn Qutaybah narrated it from Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd and made it mawqūf on Anas (his own words).

I say: It has been narrated from him both as marfūʿ and as mawqūf. Abū Saʿīd, the freed slave of Banū Hāshim, also corroborated its being marfūʿ, narrating it from Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd as marfūʿ too. It has also been narrated from the hadith of Thābit, from Anas, as marfūʿ; but Abū Ḥātim said: It is munkar (objectionable).

It has also been narrated from the hadith of Abū Dharr. Imam Aḥmad recorded it through the narration of Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Maʿdīkarib, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet ﷺ, who narrates it from his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic; and he mentioned it with the same meaning.
Some narrated it from Shahr, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ghanm, from Abū Dharr; and it has been said to be from Shahr, from Umm al-Dardāʾ, from Abū al-Dardāʾ, from the Prophet ﷺ, but that is not correct.

It has been narrated from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Ṭabarānī recorded it through the narration of Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ.
Part of it has been narrated by other routes. Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of al-Maʿrūr ibn Suwayd, from Abū Dharr, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah the Exalted says:

Whoever draws near to Me by a hand's span, I draw near to him by a forearm's length; whoever draws near to Me by a forearm's length, I draw near to him by an arm's span; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running; and whoever meets Me with nearly an earthful of sins, associating nothing with Me, I meet him with nearly an earthful of forgiveness.”

Imam Aḥmad recorded through the narration of Akhshan al-Sadūsī, who said: I went in to see Anas, and he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “By the One in whose hand is my soul, if you sinned until your sins filled what is between heaven and earth, and then asked Allah's forgiveness, He would forgive you.”
The hadith of Anas with which we began, then, contains three means by which forgiveness is attained.
The first is supplication with hope. Supplication is commanded, and an answer is promised for it, as the Exalted says: “Your Lord has said: Call on Me; I will answer you” [Ghāfir 40:60].
In the four Sunan, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Supplication is worship,” and then he recited this verse.
In another hadith, which al-Ṭabarānī recorded as marfūʿ: “Whoever is granted supplication is granted the answer,
for Allah the Exalted says: ‘Call on Me; I will answer you.’”
And in another hadith: “Allah would not open the door of supplication for a servant and close the door of the answer to him.”

Supplication, however, is a cause that brings about the answer only when its conditions are complete and its impediments absent. Its answer may fail to come because one of its conditions is missing or one of its impediments is present. Some of its conditions, impediments and etiquette were mentioned earlier, in the commentary on Hadith 10.

Among the most important of its conditions are presence of heart and hope of an answer from Allah the Exalted, as al-Tirmidhī recorded from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Call on Allah while you are certain of the answer, for Allah does not accept the supplication of a heedless, distracted heart.”
In the Musnad, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “These hearts are vessels,
and some hold more than others. So when you ask Allah, ask Him while you are certain of the answer, for Allah does not answer a servant's supplication made by rote from a heedless heart.”
That is why the servant is forbidden to say in his supplication, “O Allah, forgive me if You will”; rather, let him be firm in his request, for no one can compel Allah.

He is also forbidden to be hasty and to abandon supplication because the answer seems slow in coming. That has been made one of the impediments to the answer, so that the servant should not cut off his hope of being answered, however long it takes; for He, Glorified is He, loves those who are persistent in supplication.
It has come in the reports that when a servant whom his Lord loves calls on Him, He says: Jibrīl, do not hasten to fulfil My servant's need,

for I love to hear his voice. And the Exalted says: “Call on Him in fear and hope; truly the mercy of Allah is near to those who do good” [al-Aʿrāf 7:56]. So long as the servant persists in supplication

and hopes for the answer without cutting off hope, he is near to being answered; and whoever keeps knocking at the door will soon have it opened for him. In al-Ḥākim's Ṣaḥīḥ, from Anas as marfūʿ: “Do not fall short in supplication, for no one will perish while he supplicates.”

Among the most important things a servant asks his Lord for is the forgiveness of his sins, or what entails it, such as salvation from the Fire and entry into Paradise. The Prophet ﷺ said: “It is around these that we murmur,” meaning around asking for Paradise and salvation from the Fire.
Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī said: Whenever a supplication occurred to me and I remembered the Fire, I turned it into seeking refuge from it.

Part of Allah the Exalted's mercy towards His servant is that the servant asks Him for some worldly need and He keeps it from him and gives him something better in its place: either He averts some evil from him by it, or stores it up for him in the Hereafter, or forgives him a sin by it,
as in the Musnad and al-Tirmidhī, from the hadith of Jābir, the Prophet ﷺ said:
“No one makes a supplication but Allah gives him what he asked for or keeps from him an equivalent evil, so long as he does not ask for something sinful or for the severing of family ties.”

In the Musnad and al-Ḥākim's Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū Saʿīd, the Prophet ﷺ said: “No Muslim makes a supplication in which there is no sin or severing of family ties but Allah gives him by it one of three things:
either He hastens his supplication for him, or He stores it up for him in the Hereafter, or He removes from him an equivalent evil.” They said: Then we will ask for more.
He said: “Allah has more.”
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it, and his version has, “or He forgives him by it a sin he committed in the past,” instead of his words,
“or He removes from him an equivalent evil.”
Al-Tirmidhī also recorded, from the hadith of ʿUbādah as marfūʿ, something similar to the hadith of Abū Saʿīd.

In any case, persistence in supplicating for forgiveness, together with hope in Allah the Exalted, brings about forgiveness. Allah the Exalted says: “I am as My servant thinks of Me, so let him think of Me as he wishes”; and in one narration: “So think nothing of Allah but good.”

It is narrated from the hadith of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿUmar, as marfūʿ: “Allah the Exalted will bring the believer on the Day of Resurrection and draw him near until He places him under His veil, screened from all creation. He will say to him: Read your record. And He will make him acknowledge one sin after another: Do you recognise it? Do you recognise it?
He will say: Yes, yes. Then the servant will look to the right and the left, and Allah the Exalted will say: No harm will come to you; My servant, you are under My cover from all My creation.

There is no one between Me and you today who can see your sins but Me. Go, for I have forgiven them for you because of one single thing out of all that you have brought Me. He will say: What is it, my Lord?
He will say: You never hoped for pardon from anyone but Me.”

Among the greatest means of forgiveness, then, is that when the servant commits a sin he hopes for its forgiveness from none but his Lord, and knows that none but He forgives sins or takes His servants to task for them.
This was mentioned earlier, in the commentary on the hadith of Abū Dharr, “My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself…”
His words, “So long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I will forgive you whatever you have done, and I do not mind,” mean: however many your sins and errors, that is not too great for Me,
and I do not consider it too much. In the Ṣaḥīḥ the Prophet ﷺ said: “When one of you supplicates, let him make his longing great, for nothing is too great for Allah.”
However great the sins of the servants may be, Allah's pardon and forgiveness are greater, far greater; the sins are small beside Allah's pardon and forgiveness.
In al-Ḥākim's Ṣaḥīḥ, from Jābir: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ saying, “Oh, my sins! Oh, my sins!” two or three times. The Prophet ﷺ said to him:

“Say: O Allah, Your forgiveness is wider than my sins, and Your mercy is more to be hoped for by me than my deeds.” He said it, and he said to him: “Again.” He said it again, and he said to him: “Again,” and he said it again. Then he said to him: “Stand up; Allah has forgiven you.”
On this someone said:
You whose sin is great, Allah's / pardon is greater than your sin;
the greatest of things, beside / Allah's pardon, grows small.
Another poet said:
My Lord, though my sins are great in number, / I know that Your pardon is greater still.
If none but those who do good may hope in You, / in whom is the wrongdoer to hope, and on whom to call?
I have no means of reaching You but hope / and Your beautiful pardon — and then, I am a Muslim.
Another poet said:
When my heart grew hard and my ways grew narrow, / I made my hope in Your pardon a ladder.
My sin seemed too great to me, but when I set it / beside Your pardon, my Lord, Your pardon was the greater.
The second means of forgiveness is seeking forgiveness (istighfār), even if the sins are great and their number reaches ʿanān al-samāʾ, which is the clouds;

it has also been said to mean as far as the eye can see of the sky. In the other narration: “If you sinned until your sins reached what is between heaven and earth, and then asked Allah's forgiveness, He would forgive you.” Istighfār is asking for forgiveness (maghfirah), and maghfirah is protection from the evil of sins together with their concealment.
Seeking forgiveness is mentioned often in the Qurʾān. Sometimes it is commanded, as in His words, Exalted is He:
“And seek the forgiveness of Allah; Allah is Forgiving, Merciful” [al-Muzzammil 73:20], and His words: “And seek your Lord's forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance” [Hūd 11:3].
Sometimes He praises those who do it, as in His words, “and those who seek forgiveness before dawn” [Āl ʿImrān 3:17], and His words,

“and before dawn they would seek forgiveness” [al-Dhāriyāt 51:18], and His words: “And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins — and who forgives sins but Allah?” [Āl ʿImrān 3:135].

And sometimes He mentions that Allah forgives whoever seeks His forgiveness, as in His words, Exalted is He: “Whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks Allah's forgiveness, will find Allah Forgiving, Merciful” [al-Nisāʾ 4:110].

Seeking forgiveness is often paired with mention of repentance, in which case seeking forgiveness means asking for forgiveness with the tongue, and repentance means giving up sins with the heart and the limbs.

Sometimes seeking forgiveness is mentioned on its own, with forgiveness made to follow from it, as in this hadith and others like it. It has been said that what is meant there is seeking forgiveness joined with repentance. It has also been said that the texts on seeking forgiveness alone are all unqualified, and are to be qualified by what is mentioned in the verse of Āl ʿImrān about not persisting;

for in it Allah promised forgiveness to whoever seeks His forgiveness for his sins and does not persist in what he did, and so all the unqualified texts on seeking forgiveness are to be read in the light of this qualified one. Someone's merely saying, “O Allah, forgive me,”

is a request for forgiveness and a supplication for it, and so its ruling is that of any other supplication: if Allah wills, He answers it and forgives the one who makes it, especially when it comes from a heart broken by sin or coincides with one of the times when supplications are answered, such as the hours before dawn and the ends of the prayers.
It is narrated that Luqmān (peace be upon him) said to his son: My son, accustom your tongue to saying, “O Allah, forgive me,” for Allah has hours in which He turns away no one who asks.
Al-Ḥasan said: Seek forgiveness often — in your houses, at your tables, on your roads, in your markets and in your gatherings, wherever you are — for you do not know when forgiveness will come down.

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded in his book Ḥusn al-Ẓann, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah as marfūʿ: “A man was lying on his back when he looked up at the sky and the stars and said: I know that you have a Lord who created you. O Allah, forgive me. And He forgave him.”

From Muwarriq, who said: There was a man who used to do evil deeds. He went out into the open country, gathered some earth and lay down on it on his back, and said: My Lord, forgive me my sins. [Allah] said: This man knows that he has a Lord who forgives and punishes. And He forgave him.

From Mughīth ibn Sumayy, who said: There was a wicked man who one day came to his senses and said: O Allah, Your forgiveness! O Allah, Your forgiveness! O Allah, Your forgiveness! Then he died, and he was forgiven.

This is supported by what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ: “A servant committed a sin and said: My Lord, I have committed a sin, so forgive me. Allah the Exalted said: My servant knows that he has a Lord who forgives sin

and takes to task for it; I have forgiven My servant. Then he remained as long as Allah willed, and then committed another sin” — and he mentioned the same as the first, twice more. In a narration of Muslim's, He said the third time: “I have forgiven My servant, so let him do as he wishes.”
The meaning is: so long as he remains in this state, seeking forgiveness whenever he sins.

It appears that what is meant is seeking forgiveness joined with not persisting. That is why the hadith of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq has the Prophet ﷺ saying: “One who seeks forgiveness has not persisted, even if he goes back [to the sin] seventy times a day.” Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded it.
As for seeking forgiveness with the tongue while the heart persists in the sin, that is a mere supplication: if Allah wills, He answers it, and if He wills, He rejects it.
Persistence may also be an impediment to the answer. In the Musnad, from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr as marfūʿ: “Woe to those who persist in what they have done while they know.”

Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās as marfūʿ: “One who repents of a sin is like one who has no sin, and one who seeks forgiveness for a sin while persisting in it is like one who mocks his Lord.” Its being marfūʿ is munkar; perhaps it is mawqūf.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: There are three whose supplication is not answered — and among them he mentioned a man who keeps up an unlawful relationship with a woman. Whenever he has satisfied his desire he says: My Lord, forgive me what I did with So-and-so. And the Lord says: Leave her and I will forgive you; but so long as you keep up with her,

I will not forgive you. And a man who holds other people's wealth while seeing its owners, and says: My Lord, forgive me what I consume of So-and-so's wealth. And the Exalted says: Return their wealth to them and I will forgive you; but so long as you have not returned it to them, I will not forgive you.

Someone's saying, “I seek Allah's forgiveness,” means: I ask for His forgiveness; so it is like saying, “O Allah, forgive me.” The complete seeking of forgiveness, which brings about forgiveness, is that which is joined with not persisting, as Allah praised those who do it and promised them forgiveness.

One of those who know Allah said: Whoever's seeking of forgiveness does not bear the fruit of a sound repentance is lying in his seeking of forgiveness. One of them used to say: This seeking of forgiveness of ours needs much seeking of forgiveness. On this someone said:
I seek Allah's forgiveness for saying, “I seek Allah's forgiveness” — / a word that escaped me while I went against its meaning.
How can I hope for my supplications to be answered, / when with sin I have blocked their channel to Allah?

The best seeking of forgiveness, then, is that which is joined with abandoning persistence; it is then a sincere repentance. If he says with his tongue, “I seek Allah's forgiveness,” without having given up the sin in his heart, he is supplicating to Allah for forgiveness, as when he says, “O Allah, forgive me,”

and that is good, and he may hope to be answered. As for the one who called it the repentance of liars, he meant that it is not repentance, as some people believe it to be; and that is true, for repentance cannot coexist with persistence.
If he says, “I seek Allah's forgiveness and I repent to Him,” he is in one of two states.
The first is that he persists in the sin in his heart. Such a person is lying in saying
“and I repent to Him”, because he is not repenting, and it is not permissible for him to state of himself that he is repenting when he is not.

The second is that he has given up the sin in his heart. People differ over whether he may say, “and I repent to Him.” A group of the Salaf disliked it, and it is the view of the followers of Abū Ḥanīfah, which al-Ṭaḥāwī related from them. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said:

His saying, “and I repent to Him,” becomes a lie and a sin; rather, let him say, “O Allah, accept my repentance,” or, “O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness, so accept my repentance.” This may be taken as referring to one who has not given up the sin in his heart, and that fits his situation better.

Muḥammad ibn Sūqah used to say in his seeking of forgiveness: I seek the forgiveness of Allah the Mighty, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Sustaining, and I ask Him for sincere repentance.
It is narrated that Ḥudhayfah said: It is lie enough for a man to say, “I seek Allah's forgiveness,” and then go back to the sin.
Muṭarrif heard a man saying, “I seek Allah's forgiveness and I repent to Him,” and grew angry with him, and said: Perhaps you will not do it.
The apparent sense of this indicates that he disliked only his saying, “and I repent to Him,”
because sincere repentance means never returning to the sin, so whenever he returns to it he has lied in saying, “I repent to Him.”
Likewise Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī was asked about someone who pledged to Allah never to return to a sin, and he said:

Who is more sinful than he? He presumes to swear to Allah that His decree will not take effect in him. Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī preferred his view on this, and something similar is narrated from Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah.
The majority of scholars hold that one who repents may say, “I repent to Allah,” and that the servant may pledge to his Lord never to return to the sin,

since the resolve to do so is obligatory on him, and he is stating what he resolves at present. That is why he said: “One who seeks forgiveness has not persisted, even if he goes back seventy times a day.”
And he said, of one who returns to the sin: “I have forgiven My servant, so let him do as he wishes.”

In the hadith on the expiation of a gathering: “I seek Your forgiveness, O Allah, and I repent to You.” The Prophet ﷺ had a thief's hand cut off and then said to him: “Seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him.” He said: I seek Allah's forgiveness and I repent to Him. He said: “O Allah, accept his repentance.” Abū Dāwūd recorded it.

A number of the Salaf considered it recommended to add to the words, “I seek Allah's forgiveness and I repent to Him.” It is narrated of ʿUmar that he heard a man say, “I seek Allah's forgiveness and I repent to Him,”
and said to him: You little fool! Say: [I repent with] the repentance of one who has no power over harm or benefit for himself, nor over death, life or resurrection.

Al-Awzāʿī was asked about seeking forgiveness: Should one say, “I seek the forgiveness of Allah, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Sustaining, and I repent to Him”? He said: That is good; but let him say, “My Lord, forgive me,” so that the seeking of forgiveness is complete.

The best kind of seeking forgiveness is for the servant to begin by praising his Lord, then follow with acknowledgement of his sin, and then ask Allah for forgiveness, as in the hadith of Shaddād ibn Aws, from the Prophet ﷺ: “The master of all seeking of forgiveness is that the servant says:

O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant, and I keep to Your covenant and Your promise as far as I am able. I seek refuge with You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge before You Your favour upon me, and I acknowledge my sin; so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.” Al-Bukhārī recorded it.
In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Messenger of Allah, teach me a supplication to make in my prayer.
He said: “Say: O Allah, I have wronged myself greatly, and none forgives sins but You; so forgive me with forgiveness from You, and have mercy on me. You are the Forgiving, the Merciful.”
Among the kinds of seeking forgiveness is for the servant to say: “I seek the forgiveness of Allah, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Sustaining, and I repent to Him.”
It is narrated of the Prophet ﷺ that whoever says it is forgiven, even if he has fled from the advancing army.
Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī recorded it.
In al-Nasāʾī's book al-Yawm wa-l-Laylah, from Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt, who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, how should we seek forgiveness?

He said: “Say: O Allah, forgive us, have mercy on us and accept our repentance; You are the Accepter of repentance, the Merciful.” It also has, from Abū Hurayrah: I have never seen anyone who said, “I seek Allah's forgiveness and I repent to Him,” more often than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
In the four Sunan, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: We used to count the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying, a hundred times in a single sitting:
“My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance; You are the Accepter of repentance, the Forgiving.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “By Allah, I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him more than seventy times a day.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from al-Agharr al-Muzanī, the Prophet ﷺ said: “A veil comes over my heart, and I seek Allah's forgiveness a hundred times a day.”
In the Musnad, from Ḥudhayfah, who said: I said: Messenger of Allah, I have a sharp tongue, and most of it falls on my family. He said: “Where are you in regard to seeking forgiveness?
I seek Allah's forgiveness a hundred times in every day and night.”

In the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd, from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever seeks forgiveness often, Allah will make for him relief from every worry and a way out of every difficulty, and will provide for him from where he does not expect.”
Abū Hurayrah said: I seek Allah's forgiveness and repent to Him a thousand times every day, and that is according to the measure of my blood money.
ʿĀʾishah said: Blessed is the one who finds much seeking of forgiveness in his record.
Abū al-Minhāl said: A servant has no neighbour in his grave dearer to him than much seeking of forgiveness.
In short, the remedy for sins is seeking forgiveness. We have narrated, from the hadith of Abū Dharr as marfūʿ: “Every disease has a remedy, and the remedy for sins is seeking forgiveness.”
Qatādah said: This Qurʾān shows you your disease and your remedy. Your disease is sins, and your remedy is seeking forgiveness.
One of them said: The only resort of sinners is weeping and seeking forgiveness; whoever is troubled by his sins, let him seek forgiveness for them often.
Riyāḥ al-Qaysī said: I have some forty-odd sins, and I have sought Allah's forgiveness for each sin a hundred thousand times.

One of them took account of himself from the time he reached puberty, and found that his slips did not exceed thirty-six. He sought Allah's forgiveness for each slip a hundred thousand times and prayed a thousand rakʿahs for each slip,

completing a full recitation of the Qurʾān in every one of those rakʿahs. He said: Even so, I do not feel safe from my Lord's might, that He will not take me to task for them, and I am in peril as to whether my repentance will be accepted.
One whose concern over his sins grows may cling to the coat-tails of someone with fewer sins and ask him to seek forgiveness for him.

ʿUmar used to ask children to seek forgiveness for him, saying: You have not sinned. Abū Hurayrah used to say to the boys of the Qurʾān school: Say, “O Allah, forgive Abū Hurayrah,” and he would say āmīn to their supplication.
Bakr al-Muzanī said: If a man went round from door to door, as a beggar does, saying, “Seek forgiveness for me,” it would be fitting for him to do so.

When someone's sins and evil deeds have grown so many that they are past counting, let him seek Allah's forgiveness for what Allah knows; for Allah knows everything and has counted it, as the Exalted says:

“On the day Allah raises them all and informs them of what they did; Allah has counted it, while they have forgotten it” [al-Mujādilah 58:6]. In the hadith of Shaddād ibn Aws, from the Prophet ﷺ: “I ask You for the good of what You know,
and I seek refuge with You from the evil of what You know, and I seek Your forgiveness for what You know; You are the Knower of the unseen.”
On this someone said:
I seek Allah's forgiveness for what Allah knows; / the wretched one is he on whom Allah has no mercy.
How forbearing Allah is with one who is not mindful of Him! / All do wrong, yet Allah is forbearing.
So I seek Allah's forgiveness for whatever slips there have been; / blessed is he who refrains from what Allah dislikes.
Blessed is he whose inner self is good; / blessed is he who stops at what Allah has forbidden.
The third means of forgiveness is tawḥīd, and it is the greatest of them. Whoever lacks it lacks forgiveness, and whoever brings it has brought the greatest means of forgiveness. The Exalted says:

“Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills” [al-Nisāʾ 4:48]. Whoever brings, along with tawḥīd, nearly an earthful of sins (qurāb al-arḍ is its fill, or nearly its fill),

Allah will meet him with nearly an earthful of forgiveness. This, however, is subject to the will of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: if He wills, He forgives him, and if He wills, He takes him to task for his sins; but in the end he will not abide in the Fire forever, but will come out of it and then enter Paradise.

One of them said: The one who affirms tawḥīd is not cast into the Fire as the disbelievers are cast, does not meet in it what the disbelievers meet, and does not remain in it as the disbelievers remain. If the servant's tawḥīd, and his sincerity to Allah in it, are complete,

and he fulfils all its conditions with his heart, tongue and limbs — or with his heart and tongue at death — that brings about the forgiveness of all his past sins and keeps him from entering the Fire altogether.

When someone's heart has realised the word of tawḥīd, it drives out of him everything besides Allah, in love, veneration, reverence, awe, fear, hope and reliance. Then all his sins and errors are burned away, even if they were like the foam of the sea; and it may even turn them into good deeds, as was mentioned earlier regarding the replacement of evil deeds with good ones.
For this tawḥīd is the supreme elixir: if a single atom of it were placed on mountains of sins and errors, it would turn them into good deeds. Thus in the Musnad and elsewhere,
from Umm Hāniʾ, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Lā ilāha illā Allāh leaves no sin, and no deed surpasses it.”
In the Musnad, from Shaddād ibn Aws and ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit: The Prophet ﷺ said to his Companions: “Raise your hands and say: lā ilāha illā Allāh.” We raised our hands for a while;

then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lowered his hand and said: “Praise be to Allah. O Allah, You sent me with this word, commanded me with it and promised me Paradise for it, and You do not break Your promise.” Then he said:
“Rejoice, for Allah has forgiven you.”

Al-Shiblī said: Whoever relies on this world, it burns him with its fire and he becomes ashes scattered by the winds. Whoever relies on the Hereafter, it burns him with its light and he becomes red gold that is put to use. And whoever relies on Allah, the light of tawḥīd burns him and he becomes a jewel beyond price.

When the fire of love takes hold of the heart, it burns away from it everything besides the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. The heart is then purified of all others and becomes fit to be a throne for tawḥīd: “My heavens and My earth could not contain Me, but the heart of My believing servant contains Me.”
Longing for them has choked me on my own breath; / oh, my burning in love, oh, my burning!
Love has cast me into the depths of a sea; / so, by Allah, take the drowning man's hand!
Love for you has settled in the core of my heart / and untied every firm knot in me.

This is the last of the hadiths the Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) gave in this book. With Allah's help and by His will, we shall now give the rest of the fifty hadiths that bring together kinds of knowledge, wisdom and manners, as was promised at the beginning of the book. Allah is the One who grants success in reaching what is right.
